# Negative numbers (`negative_numbers`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: helped by zero_place_value, double_entry
- Core idea: Numbers continue below zero: a debt is a negative fortune, a position left of the starting mark has negative displacement when right is positive. The rules are that subtracting a negative is adding, a negative times a positive is negative, and a negative times a negative is positive. With them every subtraction has an answer, one formula covers cases that needed several, and equations may have negative solutions that mean something (a loss, the opposite direction). A number line drawn through zero, or a ledger of credits and debts, makes the idea concrete.
- Pitfalls:
  - Stating that minus times minus gives minus, or being unable to justify the rule (cancelling a debt three times over is a gain).
  - Assuming educated Europeans accepted them early. Cardano called them fictitious in 1545 and respected mathematicians still rejected them around 1800.
  - Confusing the minus sign of subtraction with the sign of a negative number.
  - Taking square roots of negative numbers as if they were ordinary numbers.
- History: china: c. 1st c. AD – Nine Chapters, ch. 8, rules for positive and negative (red and black rods) in elimination; AD 263 Liu Hui's commentary; india: 628 – Brahmagupta gives the rules for 'fortunes' and 'debts', including products and negative roots; greece: c. AD 250 – Diophantus calls an equation with a negative solution absurd; islamic: 10th c. – Abu'l-Wafa uses a negative result as a debt; algebraists generally avoid negative solutions; 12th c. al-Samaw'al states the sign rules; europe: 1225 – Fibonacci reads a negative solution as a debt (Flos); 1545 Cardano uses but distrusts them; full acceptance in the 18th–19th c. (Euler's Algebra, 1770)
- Read:
  - Shen Kangshen, John N. Crossley & Anthony W.-C. Lun, The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: Companion and Commentary (1999)
  - Kim Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)
  - Leonhard Euler, Vollstaendige Anleitung zur Algebra (1770)
